title: Bach's signature
hookLine: Bach signed his scores SDG, to God alone the glory

cards: A church musician in Leipzig is up late, finishing a piece for Sunday. Choir parts, organ, strings, a hymn tune running through the middle of it all.

He has a congregation to feed and a family to feed, and the deadline is days away, not months. He gets to the last bar, draws the final double line, and then, under the music, writes three letters. S.
Not a date. Three letters, where a signature would go. His name was Johann Sebastian Bach.

teach.h: SOLI DEO GLORIA: TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.
teach.b: S. D. G. stands for three Latin words: soli Deo gloria.
To God alone the glory. It's a short way of saying that the credit for any good thing belongs to God. Bach was a Lutheran, and he wrote it at the end of scores.
At the top of some, he wrote two other letters, J.
J., for Jesu juva: Jesus, help. Help at the start, glory at the end: the whole shape of a working day in four letters. The idea has a long echo in scripture.

teach.h: NOT UNTO US, NOT UNTO US.
teach.b: The opening of Psalm 115, in the King James Bible: "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory." The psalmist says not unto us twice. It's hard to mean it the first time.

And Paul takes the idea out of the church and into the kitchen: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Bach didn't save the letters for his grandest works.
Tradition says he signed ordinary pieces too, written to a deadline for an ordinary Sunday. And some of his music for keyboard students, teaching pieces, carries a dedication along the same lines.
The glory wasn't reserved for the masterpiece. It went on the homework. Bach could be stubborn, and he argued with his employers.
The letters weren't a claim to be holy. They were a way of handing the work over when it was done.

how: Some Christian musicians, artists and writers still mark their work with S.D.G. or soli Deo gloria, and others dedicate their work to God in a short prayer before they begin.

games.q: you've just finished a piece of music for Sunday, written in a rush. how do you sign it?
o: your name, large, at the top.
nothing at all; it's only for one Sunday.
three letters at the end: to God alone the glory.
games.why: Bach wrote S. D. G. under the music: soli Deo gloria. the credit went to God, even on the homework.

practice: Pick one ordinary piece of work ahead of you, an email, a meal, a shift, a conversation with a child, and picture finishing it and quietly signing it, the way Bach signed his scores. If you pray, whisper S. D.
G. at the end, or the psalm, not unto us, O Lord; if not, sign it for the person it serves, and let the credit go.

wordCard.voice: Bach's signature. The letters S. D. G., soli Deo gloria, to God alone the glory, written by Johann Sebastian Bach at the end of his scores.
